subject: Cloud Computing
title: Multi-Factor Authentication
description: A quick, practical guide to Multi-Factor Authentication.

hook.text: A hacker steals your password. Without MFA, they walk right into your cloud account. With it, they're stuck.

buildup.text: MFA requires two or more factors: something you know (password), something you have (phone), or something you are.

discovery.text: Cloud providers offer MFA through apps, hardware keys, and SMS. Hardware keys are the most secure option.

twist.text: Despite being critical, many cloud root accounts still lack MFA. It's the simplest fix most teams skip.

climax.text: AWS reported that enabling MFA on root accounts blocks 99% of account compromise attempts.

punchline.text: MFA takes 30 seconds to enable. It stops 99% of attacks.

quiz.question: Why is MFA especially important for cloud root accounts?
options: Root accounts have unlimited access and are prime targets for attackers
MFA is only available for root accounts, not regular users
Cloud providers charge less if MFA is enabled on root

details.summary: MFA requires two or more verification factors to authenticate: something you know, something you have, or something you are. It blocks over 99 percent of automated credential attacks and is considered essential for all cloud accounts.
details.whyItMatters: Passwords alone are easily compromised through phishing, reuse, and brute force. MFA is the single most effective defense against account takeover in cloud environments.
takeaways: MFA blocks over 99 percent of automated credential attacks
Combines knowledge, possession, and biometric factors
Should be mandatory for all cloud administrative accounts

faq.question: Which MFA methods are most secure?
faq.answer: Hardware security keys like YubiKeys are the strongest, followed by authenticator apps that generate time-based codes. SMS-based codes are weakest because phone numbers can be hijacked through SIM swapping attacks.

faq.question: Should MFA be required for all users or just admins?
faq.answer: All users should have MFA enabled. Attackers often compromise low-privilege accounts first, then escalate. Requiring MFA universally prevents the most common entry point: stolen or phished passwords from any account level.
